traits.notes: The seedling exhibits compound, odd-pinnate leaves with 7 leaflets arranged alternately along the rachis. The stem is woody and smooth, with visible tendrils emerging from leaf axils, suggesting a climbing habit. Some leaflets show minor damage with small holes and spots, but no clear signs of insect or pathogen activity. The plant is growing in leaf litter, with no clear indication of habitat type beyond ground-level debris. The pink tag and plastic bag are artificial artifacts and not part of the plant. Tendrils are clearly visible in multiple images, confirming their presence.

=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): alternate (leaves are attached at successive nodes along the stem, alternating sides; no paired or clustered arrangement visible at any node)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): distal (leaves are spaced along the stem with visible internodes, not clustered at the apex)
B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): compound (each leaf unit is composed of multiple leaflets attached to a central rachis)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): odd-pinnate (the terminal leaflet is present, and leaflets are arranged along the rachis in pairs with one at the end)
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): 7 (each compound leaf has 3 pairs of lateral leaflets plus one terminal leaflet, totaling 7 leaflets)
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): alternate (leaflets are arranged alternately along the rachis, not in pairs at the same node)
C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (margins are smooth without teeth or lobes)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): lanceolate (leaflets are elongated with a broad base tapering to a pointed tip)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (tip is sharply pointed but not drawn out into a long tail)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): cuneate (base is wedge-shaped, tapering to the petiole)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (primary vein runs centrally with secondary veins branching off to the sides)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, closely spaced, numerous (secondary veins are clearly visible, running parallel to each other and close together)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): shiny (surface has a glossy appearance, reflecting light)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs or trichomes on the leaf surface)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petiole is short, connecting leaflet to rachis without elongation)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (petiole is round in cross-section, not flattened or winged)
D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): woody (stem appears firm and slightly lignified, typical of young woody vines or trees)
    18. Stem trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs on stem surface)
    19. Stem color: green to dark green (stem is green, transitioning to darker green or brownish near base)
    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): smooth (surface is smooth without ridges or lenticels)
E. Other Visible Seedling Traits
    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipules observed at leaf base)
    22. Latex, rarely visible but extremely diagnostic when present (present / not observed): not observed (no exudate seen when stem or leaf is damaged)
    23. Pulvinus, for Fabaceae family only (present / absent): absent (no swollen base at leaflet or leaf attachment point)
    24. Tendrils (present / absent): present (thin, coiled structures emerging from leaf axils, likely tendrils for climbing)
F. Notes: The seedling exhibits compound, odd-pinnate leaves with 7 leaflets arranged alternately along the rachis. The stem is woody and smooth, with visible tendrils emerging from leaf axils, suggesting a climbing habit. Some leaflets show minor damage with small holes and spots, but no clear signs of insect or pathogen activity. The plant is growing in leaf litter, with no clear indication of habitat type beyond ground-level debris. The pink tag and plastic bag are artificial artifacts and not part of the plant. Tendrils are clearly visible in multiple images, confirming their presence.
